"Delt" is an informal, shortened form of "deltoid" — specifically the deltoid muscle, which is the large, prominent muscle that wraps around the top of your shoulder and gives it its rounded, dome-like shape.

Place your hand on the top of your shoulder — that fleshy, rounded mass sitting right there, capping the joint where your arm meets your torso — that is your delt. It covers the shoulder joint from the front, side, and back, almost like a thick shoulder pad.

The delt is shaped roughly like a triangle or an inverted fan — wide at the top where it attaches to the collarbone and shoulder blade, and narrowing into a point where it attaches to the upper arm bone (the humerus). When well-developed, it gives the shoulder a full, round, cannonball-like appearance.

The delt is the primary muscle responsible for lifting your arm. It allows you to:

  • Raise your arm directly in front of you (like reaching for a shelf ahead of you)
  • Raise your arm out to the side (like a jumping jack motion)
  • Swing your arm behind you (like reaching backward)
  • Rotate your arm in various directions

In short: almost every time you move your arm away from your body, your delt is involved.
The three parts of a delt

The delt is divided into three distinct sections, each responsible for a slightly different movement. You'll often hear these referred to as "heads":

  1. Front delt (anterior head) — Located at the front of the shoulder. It helps lift your arm forward (e.g., raising your arm to point at something in front of you). It also gets worked heavily during pushing movements like push-ups or bench pressing.
  2. Side delt (lateral head) — Located on the outer side of the shoulder. This is the part most responsible for the wide, rounded look of the shoulder. It lifts your arm out to the side. When people talk about building "broad shoulders," they're largely talking about developing this part.
  3. Rear delt (posterior head) — Located at the back of the shoulder. It helps pull your arm backward and is important for good posture and shoulder stability. This part is often the most underdeveloped in people who sit at desks or do a lot of pushing exercises without balancing them with pulling exercises.

"Delt" is casual, informal vocabulary. You'll hear it most often in:

  • Fitness and gym culture — This is the primary setting where the word is used. Gym-goers, personal trainers, bodybuilders, and athletes routinely use it instead of the more formal "deltoid."
  • Sports commentary and coaching
  • Physical therapy and rehabilitation contexts (though therapists more often use the full word "deltoid")

It is almost always used in the plural form "delts" when speaking generally about both shoulders:

"My delts are sore from yesterday's workout."
"She has incredibly developed delts."
"I'm going to train delts and arms today."

The singular "delt" is used when referring to one shoulder specifically, or to one of its three sections:

"I pulled my left delt."
"Your rear delt is lagging behind the other two."

You'll also hear it used as a modifier (acting like an adjective) in phrases like:

"delt day" (a workout day dedicated to shoulder training)
"delt exercises"
"front delt raise" (a specific exercise)

It's worth being clear: "delt" always refers to a muscle, not to the entire shoulder joint or bone structure. The shoulder is a complex system of bones, joints, tendons, and muscles. When someone says "delt," they mean only the deltoid muscle — not the rotator cuff, not the shoulder blade, not the collarbone, not the ball-and-socket joint itself.

If you want to remember this word in one sentence:

Your delt is the rounded muscle capping your shoulder that lets you lift and move your arm in most directions.

It's a casual gym word. Hear someone say "I'm training delts today" — they mean they're working out their shoulder muscles.
